rationale: The chomp benchmark is a small integer/game-tree search program from the McGill suite: it has small hot recursive search loops, no large data structures, and an empty profile indicating minimal static insight, so the weight table favors cheap, low-risk transformations and tempers aggressive ones. SUB and SPLIT get the highest SecurityGain/DiversityGain weights with near-zero cost/risk weights because they degrade pattern matching at negligible runtime/size penalty, ideal for small hot functions. FLA and BCF get moderate weights — they add strong control-flow resistance, but their runtime/size weights are kept elevated enough that the selector will de-prioritize them on hot recursive game-search functions where the cost dimension dominates. IBR and ICALL have solid security value (breaking branch/call-target static analysis, which is very effective against small binaries) but carry higher CorrectnessRisk and indirect-call overhead, so they are enabled at moderate weights. IGV is enabled moderately to hide the game board/global state access patterns, with its CorrectnessRisk weight raised slightly since global indirection can interact badly with linkage if applied too liberally. Overall: maximize structural obfuscation on cold functions, restrict heavyweight transforms on hot paths.
